summary:
Mission Mars 1.0 is a planetary surface exploration and path-planning platform that helps plan safer astronaut EVAs and autonomous rover traverses on Mars.

What we developed: A web-based mission control tool with two parts. The React + Leaflet frontend streams NASA JPL Mars Trek imagery (Viking optical, MOLA color relief, THEMIS thermal IR) with live telemetry. The FastAPI backend runs slope-constrained A* pathfinding directly on the full 463 m/pixel NASA MGS MOLA global elevation dataset. Memory-mapped slicing keeps resident RAM near zero, so routing works between any two coordinates on Mars. Users choose a traverse profile (Safest, Science, or Fastest) and receive a route with distance, elevation gain, maximum slope, estimated EVA time, and a SAFE / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict.

How it addresses the challenge: Instead of guessing routes from image brightness, which can lead into cliffs, we compute true physical slope from elevation data, corrected for latitude. Routes avoid terrain beyond biomechanical and rover limits.

Why it matters: Mars has extreme relief, and a poorly planned traverse risks oxygen overuse, equipment strain, or rollover. Our platform gives mission planners fast, physics-grounded, explainable routing that runs on lightweight cloud servers and ships as a ready-to-run Docker image.
details:
What it does and how it works

Mission Mars 1.0 lets a user pick any two coordinates on Mars and get a terrain-aware route between them. The user selects start and end points on an interactive map, chooses a traverse profile, and receives a path with telemetry and a safety verdict.

Under the hood:

  1. Visualization: The React frontend streams NASA JPL Mars Trek WMTS tiles (Viking 232 m optical, MOLA 463 m color relief, THEMIS 100 m day IR) in an equirectangular projection.
  2. Slicing: A request goes to our FastAPI backend, which cuts the needed bounding box from the full 23,040 × 46,080 MOLA elevation raster. The raster is memory-mapped, so only the required cells are read from disk. Local routes keep every native 463 m cell, while continent-scale routes are strided to roughly 300 × 300 cells.
  3. Pathfinding: A custom A* engine computes the true slope between every pair of neighboring cells, correcting for latitude foreshortening (cos φ), and blocks steps above each profile’s slope limit.
  4. Output: The API returns waypoints with elevation and slope, total distance, elevation gain, max slope, estimated EVA time, and a SAFE / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict with a plain-language reason.

Three traverse profiles:

  • Safest: 8° slope limit (relaxing to 14° only if blocked), with heavy penalties on climbs, so routes follow flat valleys around crater rims and canyon walls.
  • Science: 12° limit, with a 60% cost discount near sites like Jezero, Gale, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, Elysium, and Hellas.
  • Fastest: 22° limit, minimizing distance while still refusing sheer cliffs.

Benefits

  • Routes are grounded in real elevation physics rather than image brightness, which can mislead (dark pixels can be flat sand or shadow, bright pixels can be steep sunlit walls).
  • Planners see explainable results: every route carries a verdict, the reason behind it, and per-waypoint slope.
  • It is lightweight and cheap to run. Near-zero resident RAM and sub-40 ms routing for large areas mean it works on a small cloud instance instead of a GPU or high-memory server.
  • It is easy to deploy, shipped as a pre-built Docker image with the processed elevation data included.

Intended impact

We want to make EVA and rover traverse planning faster, safer, and more accessible. Poor route choices on Mars can cause oxygen overuse, spacesuit joint strain, and rover rollover. A tool that quantifies slope risk across the whole planet helps mission planners, researchers, students, and future explorers compare options before committing to a route. Because it is open and lightweight, it can also serve as an educational platform for planetary science.

Tools, languages, and technologies

  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet; deployed on Vercel’s edge CDN
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, Pydantic v2
  • Data: NASA MGS MOLA MEGDR global DEM (463 m/px), Viking MDIM 2.1 color mosaic, MOLA color shaded relief, 2001 Mars Odyssey THEMIS day IR (all from NASA JPL / USGS Astrogeology)
  • Data preparation: One-time GeoTIFF → .npy (int16) conversion with Rasterio, so production needs no GDAL or Rasterio
  • Infrastructure: Docker, Docker Hub, AWS EC2 (Amazon Linux) with a configured security group
  • Hardware: Standard laptops for development and a single EC2 instance for hosting. No specialized hardware.

What makes it creative

  • Decoupling visuals from physics: Imagery is for the human eye, while elevation data drives the routing.
  • Memory-mapped global DEM: Instead of loading a 2 GB raster into RAM, we treat it as a virtual array on disk, which makes planet-scale routing practical on small servers.
  • Mission-aware cost functions: Three distinct profiles reflect different operational goals, including a science mode that biases routes toward sites of geological interest.
  • Intentionally raw A* paths: We skip curve smoothing so every ridge detour and elevation sample from the DEM is preserved, keeping the path honest and verifiable.
  • Antimeridian-aware rendering: Polylines are split correctly where routes cross ±180° longitude, a detail many map tools get wrong on a planetary scale.

Factors our team considered

  • Physical realism: Latitude-corrected metric distances, real slope angles, and thresholds tied to human biomechanics (metabolic cost, suit torque) and rover stability.
  • Safety and honesty: Conservative verdict thresholds (SAFE ≤ 6°, CAUTION up to 15°, NO-GO beyond) and clear reporting when a path is blocked, rather than returning an unsafe route silently.
  • Performance and cost: Memory-mapping, stride-based downsampling for large routes, and a pre-baked container to avoid heavy per-deploy processing.
  • Data fidelity and limits: At 463 m/pixel, small hazards like boulders and sub-pixel cliffs are not resolved, so the tool is best for strategic route planning and could later be paired with higher-resolution data (such as HiRISE) for tactical planning.
  • Usability: A HUD-style interface with layer switching, a landmarks list, search, and telemetry cards so non-experts can read results at a glance.
  • Reproducibility: Open documentation, a defined API, and a Docker image so others can run, verify, and extend the project.
